To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cold-sensitive cytosol binding proteins from human red blood cell membranes undergo a reversible molecular transformation between polymeric and monomeric forms.
the 60-kDa monomeric form of CTBP IV is the inactive precursor form of all the CTBPs, and is converted to the polymeric forms by heat, cold and pH treatments.
cold, heat and isothermic pH treatments affect the molecular interconversion of cytosolic 2,3,5-tri-ido-L-thyronin binding proteins from human eryrocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interconversion of the cold-sensitive CTBPs from human red cells.
the molecular mechanism of the interconversion of the cold-sensitive cytosolically distributed thyroid hormone-binding proteins from human red blood cell.
the effect of cold, pH, and temperature on the molecular interconversion of CTBP I, CTBP II, and CTBP IV from human erythroctyes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cold-sensitive CTBP IV is a polymeric form of CTBP I and II and that the interconversion is a result of the association-dissociations of the protein.
the cold-sensitive CTBP IV species is the monomer form, and the cold-resistant CTBP I and II are the polymeric form.
the CTBPs from red blood cells exist in a dynamic state of equilibrium between the polymeric (active) and monomeric (inactive) forms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CTBP IV is the active form, and CTBPs I and II are inactive forms, of the CTBPs in red blood cells.

the cold-induced conformational change of CTBP I and II species is a reversible process, whereas the heat-induced conformational changes of CTBPs are not reversible, and that pH changes are also involved in the conformational changes.
cold treatment causes dissociation of CTBP I and II into the inactive 60 kDa monomer, which is re-activated upon warming.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CTBP IV is the only active CTBP species in human erythrocyte cytosol, and that CTBP IV can be activated by heat or pH treatment.
CTBP IV is a polymeric protein that undergoes rapid reversible dissociation at low temperatures.
CTBP IV, a cytosolic 60 kDa protein that binds to 3,3’,5-tri-ido-L-thyronin (T3), is the main form of the CTBP I and II species.
